title: DSA in Python: graphs, BFS/DFS and topological sort
seriesDescription: Hashing, windows, stacks, binary search, lists, trees, heaps and graphs with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Python graph code: adjacency lists and their shared-list trap, grid DFS, Kahn's algorithm with deque, three-colour cycle detection and the recursion limit.
source: Python documentation (collections.deque, defaultdict, sys.setrecursionlimit); LeetCode problem set; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `build_graph(n, edges)` that returns an adjacency list (a list of lists) for an undirected graph with vertices `0..n-1`.

questions.explanation: Build each inner list separately with a comprehension. `[[]] * n` would put the same list in every slot.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `num_islands(grid)` for a grid of `"1"` (land) and `"0"` (water) strings; count the 4-directionally connected groups of land. You may modify the grid.

checks.label: scans every cell with nested loops
starts a search only from unvisited land
marks visited cells (sink the land or use a set)
explores the four neighbours with a bounds check
increments a counter once per island

questions.explanation: Sinking visited land acts as the visited set. For big grids use an explicit stack or deque, because the default recursion limit is about 1000 frames.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `has_cycle(n, edges)` for a directed graph with nodes 0..n-1 (edges are `(u, v)` pairs) using DFS with three states per node: unvisited, on the current path, finished.

checks.label: keeps a state or colour per node
treats a node on the current path as a cycle
marks a node finished after exploring it
returns True when a cycle is found

questions.explanation: Meeting a node that is still on the current path is a back edge, which is exactly a cycle. Meeting a finished node is harmless.

questions.prompt: Match each Python structure with its role in graph algorithms.

left.text: `dict from old node to new node`

right.text: The BFS queue (and Kahn's ready queue)
An adjacency list built on demand for sparse graphs
The frontier of Dijkstra's algorithm, ordered by distance
Original-to-copy lookup while cloning a graph

questions.explanation: Pick the structure that makes the main loop O(1) per step: deque for FIFO, set or list for visited, heapq for weighted frontiers.

questions.text: BFS uses a collections.{1} so that q.{2}() removes from the front in O(1); it runs in O(V + E) on an adjacency list, and marks a node visited when it is {3} so it is never queued twice.
questions.explanation: `list.pop(0)` would work but costs O(n) per call. Marking at dequeue time lets the same node sit in the queue many times.

questions.prompt: A `collections.deque q` starts as `deque([1, 2, 3])`. It then runs `q.appendleft(4), q.pop(), q.popleft(), q.appendleft(5)`. What does `q[-1]` return?
questions.explanation: After `appendleft(4)` the deque is `[4, 1, 2, 3]`; `pop` removes 3; `popleft` removes 4, leaving `[1, 2]`; `appendleft(5)` gives `[5, 1, 2]`. The last item is 2. I ran it to confirm.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: `adj = [[]] * n` gives n independent empty adjacency lists.
questions.reason: Multiplying a list repeats references to the same inner object.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: R is true, and it is exactly why A is false: all n slots point to one list, so adj[0].append(1) shows up in every slot.

questions.explanation: Use `[[] for _ in range(n)]` or `defaultdict(list)`. The same trap appears with grids built as `[[0] * c] * r`.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: BFS written with `collections.deque` and `popleft` runs in O(V + E) on an adjacency list.

whys.a: R explains why a list is slow, not why the deque version is linear.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is about the slower alternative; the linear bound comes from handling each vertex and edge once.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: With a list as the queue each `pop(0)` is O(n), which can turn BFS into O(V * (V + E)) in the worst case.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A recursive DFS over a path graph of 5,000 nodes can raise `RecursionError` in default Python.
questions.reason: `sys.setrecursionlimit` permanently enlarges the C stack, so raising it is always safe.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option applies.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the default limit is about 1000 frames), but R is false: raising the limit does not grow the C stack, and deep recursion can still crash the interpreter.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Prefer an explicit stack for deep graphs. Raising the recursion limit is a stopgap.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A visited set of `(r, c)` tuples works for grid DFS, but a set of `[r, c]` lists raises `TypeError`.
questions.reason: Lists are mutable and therefore unhashable, while tuples of integers are hashable.

whys.a: Correct: set members must be hashable, and only the tuple version is.
whys.b: R is exactly the reason, so it does explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Alternatively encode a cell as `r * cols + c` and keep a set of integers.

questions.prompt: Which expression builds n independent empty lists to use as an adjacency list?

options.why: Correct: the comprehension evaluates `[]` once per slot, creating n separate lists.
This repeats one list object n times, so every slot is the same list.
`list()` is evaluated once and then repeated, so the slots still share one list.
`fromkeys` uses the one default object for every key, so the lists are shared.

questions.explanation: Same trap for grids: `[[0] * c for _ in range(r)]` is correct, `[[0] * c] * r` is not.

questions.prompt: A recursive DFS over a path graph of 100,000 nodes will raise `RecursionError` in default CPython, so an explicit stack or raising the limit is needed.

options.why: Correct: the default limit is about 1000 frames, far below 100,000.
The default recursion limit is far smaller than 100,000.

questions.explanation: Use an explicit list stack for iterative DFS, or raise `sys.setrecursionlimit` with care.

questions.prompt: In `[0] * n` used for in-degrees, assigning `indeg[v] += 1` on one slot changes every slot because the zeros are shared.

options.why: Integers are immutable, so `+=` rebinds one slot only.
Correct: `+=` on an `int` creates a new int and stores it in that one slot, so the sharing trap only affects mutable items like lists.

questions.explanation: So `[0] * n` is a fine counter array, whereas `[[]] * n` is not a fine array of lists.
